claims.text: An MLIP trained on carefully selected ab initio calculations can reproduce accurate free energies for both solid and liquid states.
Using such an MLIP can substantially reduce the computational cost of predicting fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties.
The proposed training calculations incorporate vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling.
The MLIP is calibrated using a limited number of high-fidelity calculations for both solid and liquid phases.
Enhanced sampling with the MLIP replaces full ab initio molecular dynamics.
The relevant testing window is approximately 10–20% below to 10–20% above the expected melting temperature.
The proposed method applies from pure elements and binaries through moderately multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
TOR-TILD begins to slow down for moderately multicomponent alloys.
The MLIP effectively captures the anharmonic potential-energy surface relevant to the free energies of both phases.
The MLIP effectively captures vibrational properties that contribute to solid and liquid free energies.
Training on selected ab initio data enables the MLIP to learn vibrational-entropy and electron–vibration-coupling contributions.
Molecular dynamics driven by the MLIP yields free-energy differences comparable to those from explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
MLIP phase free energies, melting temperatures, and latent heats will deviate by less than approximately 5–10% from full ab initio results.
The MLIP workflow will be approximately 10–100 times faster than explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
The MLIP workflow will scale better than TOR-TILD for multicomponent systems.
Reliability may deteriorate for extremely complex compositions or thermodynamic states far from melting.
Prior work has successfully reproduced ab initio potential-energy landscapes for simpler systems.
Accurate treatment of electron–vibration coupling in multicomponent high-entropy systems remains uncertain pending comparison with full ab initio results.
